data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Baker's theorem provides a bound, but not necessarily one tight enough to rule out all cycles for all n."],"overturn_conditions":["Finding a cycle that satisfies the Diophantine constraints."],"shared_structure":["Linear forms in logarithms","Approximation of irrational ratios","Bounding gaps to prevent cycles"],"source_memory_refs":["SCR_007","SCR_005"],"transfer_claims":["The impossibility of a cycle is a corollary of Baker's theorem on linear forms in logarithms."]},"claim":"The Collatz conjecture is unsettled and would be settled by proving a lower bound on the gap between powers of 2 and 3, specifically showing that |2^m - 3^k| cannot be sufficiently small to allow a non-trivial cycle.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The existence of a sequence of integers where the ratio 3^k/2^m approaches 1 faster than the growth of the sequence itself.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"Proof that the gap |2^m - 3^k| can be arbitrarily small relative to k.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The 'covering principle' is a Diophantine gap: since log 2 / log 3 is irrational (and likely has a specific transcendence type), the 'near-misses' where 3^k / 2^m \u2248 1 are too rare and too distant to support a closed loop in the integer domain.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
